title: How PM2 keeps the apps up
claim: PM2 brings an app back after a crash, a memory overrun or a reboot without anyone logging in. A person is needed only when an app keeps failing as it starts, and for a deploy.

nodes.title: PM2 daemon
nodes.desc: starts the apps saved by pm2 save

nodes.title: App running
nodes.desc: both apps follow the same rules

nodes.title: Restart it
nodes.desc: waits 3 s, starts a new process

nodes.title: Marked errored
nodes.desc: stays down until someone fixes it and runs pm2 restart

steps: When the VM boots, systemd starts NGINX, PostgreSQL and PM2. Running `pm2 startup systemd` once installed the unit that starts PM2.
PM2 comes up and reads the process list that `pm2 save` stored.
It starts the dashboard (gunicorn) and the API (uvicorn), each with only its own settings from `.env`.
PM2 notices when an app's process exits, or when it grows past `max_memory_restart: 500M`.
Unless the app has failed ten times in a row, each time within a second of starting, PM2 restarts it.
After `restart_delay` (3 seconds) a fresh process starts and the app is back, usually before anyone notices.

steps.text: Ten quick failures in a row (`max_restarts: 10`) usually means a start-up problem, such as a missing secret. PM2 stops trying and marks the app errored; `pm2 logs` shows why.
A deploy is done by hand on the VM: pull, install, stop the API while the database is backed up and any new migrations run, then reload both apps so they pick up new code and settings.

notes: Only quick failures count towards the ten. An app that runs for a while and then crashes is restarted every time. This is PM2's documented `min_uptime` behaviour (1 second by default), not something set in this repo.
PM2 restarts a process that has exited, not one that is up but not answering. The repo has no health check or uptime monitor.
Logs are rotated by `pm2-logrotate`: 10 MB a file, 7 files kept. A `git pull` alone publishes the website, but an NGINX config change also has to be copied into `/etc/nginx` and reloaded.
